exercises.title: A place worth noticing
exercises.prompt: Write one paragraph of 80–120 words about a place you know well. Choose one impression and support it with two concrete details. Finish with a sentence that returns to your main point.
exercises.focus: Help the reader picture one clear impression.

writing.audience: A classmate who has never visited the place.
writing.purpose: Help the reader picture one clear impression.
writing.outlineHint: Main impression → detail one → detail two → closing thought.

criteria.label: Purpose and audience
criteria.description: Does the draft accomplish a clear purpose for its intended reader?

anchors.emerging: The main point or intended reader is hard to identify.
anchors.developing: A purpose is visible, but some details or tone do not serve this reader.
anchors.effective: The main point is clear, and the detail and tone consistently serve the reader.

criteria.label: Organization
criteria.description: Can the reader follow the order and connections between ideas?

anchors.emerging: Ideas appear in an order the reader must reconstruct.
anchors.developing: The overall order works, but a connection or paragraph focus needs attention.
anchors.effective: Paragraphs have clear roles, and transitions explain how ideas connect.

criteria.label: Support
criteria.description: Do reasons, examples, and qualifications support the main point honestly?

anchors.emerging: Important claims lack explanation, examples, or needed qualifications.
anchors.developing: Some relevant support is present, but a claim or example needs development.
anchors.effective: Specific, relevant support connects to the point; uncertainty and hypothetical examples are labelled.

criteria.label: Clarity
criteria.description: Can the reader understand the sentences and references without guessing?

anchors.emerging: Vague references or crowded sentences obscure important meaning.
anchors.developing: Meaning is mostly clear, but a phrase or sentence still requires rereading.
anchors.effective: Precise wording and manageable sentences make the intended meaning easy to follow.

exercises.title: Explain a useful routine
exercises.prompt: Explain a simple routine that saves you time. In 120–180 words, name the goal, present the steps in order, and explain one step that a newcomer might misunderstand.
exercises.focus: Make the sequence usable without extra questions.

writing.audience: Someone trying the routine for the first time.
writing.purpose: Make the sequence usable without extra questions.
writing.outlineHint: Goal → ordered steps → tricky step → final check.

exercises.title: Give one reason that matters
exercises.prompt: A shared study room may introduce a daily quiet hour. Write 120–180 words recommending whether it should. Give one reason and a realistic example. Acknowledge one person who might find the rule difficult.
exercises.focus: Recommend a practical choice with a reason.

writing.audience: Students who share the study room.
writing.purpose: Recommend a practical choice with a reason.

exercises.title: Revise an unclear notice
exercises.prompt: Rewrite this original notice in 80–120 words: “We will do the thing next week near the usual area. Bring what you need. Some people should come early because it might take a while.” Choose reasonable event details yourself. Identify them as your own decisions rather than facts from the notice. Then explain two changes that help the reader act.
exercises.focus: Replace vague instructions with clear, honest directions.

writing.audience: A new volunteer who did not hear the earlier announcement.
writing.purpose: Replace vague instructions with clear, honest directions.

exercises.title: Teach a concept without jargon
exercises.prompt: Explain how a waiting list works to a new club member in 250–350 words. Use an everyday example, explain what happens when a place opens, and distinguish joining the list from receiving a guaranteed place.
exercises.focus: Explain a process and correct a likely misunderstanding.

writing.audience: A new member unfamiliar with registration systems.
writing.purpose: Explain a process and correct a likely misunderstanding.

exercises.title: An essay about a small experiment
exercises.prompt: Write a 350–500 word essay about a small change someone could test to improve a study routine. Establish a central idea, develop two connected sections, and explain how the person could tell whether the change helped. Avoid presenting an imagined outcome as proven evidence.
exercises.focus: Develop a focused idea with connected explanation.

writing.audience: A student looking for a realistic change to try.
writing.purpose: Develop a focused idea with connected explanation.
writing.outlineHint: Central idea → why the change may help → how to test → qualified conclusion.

exercises.title: Make a fair budget argument
exercises.prompt: A club can fund either a printer or longer access to a shared meeting space. Write 300–450 words recommending one option. Give two reasons, address a reasonable objection, and identify information that could change your recommendation. Do not invent cost figures as facts.
exercises.focus: Support a recommendation while acknowledging uncertainty.

writing.audience: Club members deciding how to spend a limited budget.
writing.purpose: Support a recommendation while acknowledging uncertainty.
writing.outlineHint: Recommendation → two reasons → objection → missing information.

exercises.title: Revise a sweeping claim
exercises.prompt: Revise this original passage into 200–300 words: “Online meetings are always better. Everyone saves time and nobody misses important information. We should stop meeting in person immediately.” Preserve a defensible main idea, qualify unsupported claims, include a concrete hypothetical example, and address a limitation. Add a brief note explaining your most important revision.
exercises.focus: Make an overconfident argument fair and supportable.

writing.audience: A mixed group that values both convenience and participation.
writing.purpose: Make an overconfident argument fair and supportable.
writing.outlineHint: Defensible claim → qualified support → example → limitation → revision note.

exercises.title: One explanation, two readers
exercises.prompt: Explain how a recommendation feed selects content in two versions: 200–250 words for a younger student and 200–250 for a community organizer. Distinguish what a system may optimize from what it can know about a person. Add a note explaining three audience-based choices.
exercises.focus: Adapt detail and language without changing the core meaning.

writing.audience: A younger student and a community organizer, in separate versions.
writing.purpose: Adapt detail and language without changing the core meaning.
writing.outlineHint: Shared core idea → student version → organizer version → adaptation note.

exercises.title: An essay that weighs a tradeoff
exercises.prompt: Write a 600–800 word essay on how a neighborhood should balance quiet space and organized activity in a public park. Define the tension, develop a coherent line of reasoning, engage a competing need fairly, and end with a qualified principle rather than a universal rule. Label hypothetical examples as hypothetical.
exercises.focus: Develop a nuanced position across several connected sections.

writing.audience: Residents with different uses for the same park.
writing.purpose: Develop a nuanced position across several connected sections.
writing.outlineHint: Tension → organizing idea → competing needs → synthesis → qualified principle.

exercises.title: Argue for a reversible policy
exercises.prompt: Propose a limited pilot for allowing flexible opening hours in a shared facility. In 500–700 words, define the decision, compare benefits and costs, address the strongest objection, and specify evidence and a stopping condition for the pilot. Distinguish value judgments from factual claims.
exercises.focus: Defend a testable recommendation while making tradeoffs visible.

writing.audience: A committee responsible for access, staffing, and fairness.
writing.purpose: Defend a testable recommendation while making tradeoffs visible.
writing.outlineHint: Proposal → criteria → tradeoffs → objection → evaluation and stopping condition.

exercises.title: Revise a false choice
exercises.prompt: Rewrite this original argument in 400–550 words: “Either our group adopts one fixed communication channel or collaboration will fail. Anyone who wants another option is refusing to cooperate.” Remove the false choice, represent a reasonable opposing view fairly, propose a workable policy, and identify what remains uncertain. Add a revision memo explaining which structural change mattered most.
exercises.focus: Rebuild the argument rather than only polishing its sentences.

writing.audience: A team whose members have different access needs and work schedules.
writing.purpose: Rebuild the argument rather than only polishing its sentences.
writing.outlineHint: Fair problem definition → alternatives → supported policy → uncertainty → revision memo.
